title: Hotspots: Hawaii and Yellowstone
objective: After this level you can explain what a hotspot is and why it leaves a chain of volcanoes as a plate moves over it.
summary: A hotspot stays roughly put while a plate slides over it, so it leaves a line of volcanoes: the Hawaiian-Emperor chain, with its bend, and Yellowstone's trail across Idaho.

cards.headline: Slide a sheet of paper over a candle and you get a line of scorch marks.
cards.body: Now swap the candle for a hotspot, a deep source of heat that stays put, and the paper for a moving plate. The scorch marks are volcanoes. Earth has several of these lines, and one runs right under a US national park.

cards.headline: Wilson's idea
cards.body: In 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson suggested that the Hawaiian chain formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a deep, stationary hotspot. A volcano grows while it sits over the heat, then gets carried away and dies. That's why each island or seamount in the chain is older toward the northwest. The line of volcanoes is a diary of the plate's journey.

cards.fact: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain has a sharp 60° bend, about 47 million years old.
cards.context: Past the bend, the chain carries on as the older Emperor chain, mostly drowned seamounts. For decades scientists argued: did the Pacific Plate change direction, or did the hotspot itself drift? A 2017 study concluded it took both. Even a 'stationary' hotspot can wander a little.

cards.headline: Yellowstone: a hotspot under a continent
cards.body: The same trick works on land. The North American Plate has been moving west-southwest over the Yellowstone hotspot, leaving a trail of volcanic fields across southern Idaho's Snake River Plain. The farther southwest you go, the older they get; the oldest, about 17 million years old, lie in northern Nevada and southern Oregon. Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs are the hotspot's current address.

cards.headline: Hotspots: tracked
learned: A plate slides over a hotspot that stays roughly put
Hawaii gets older toward the northwest

questions.prompt: Put the places on the Yellowstone hotspot's trail in order, from youngest to oldest.
questions.explanation: Yellowstone is the hotspot's current address, the fields across Idaho's Snake River Plain are older, and the oldest lie in northern Nevada and southern Oregon.

questions.prompt: Why is each Hawaiian island or seamount older toward the northwest?

options.label: The plate carries each volcano away from a hotspot that stays put
The hotspot itself races northwest, leaving the old islands behind
options.rationale: In Wilson's idea, the plate moves, not the hotspot.

options.label: Islands in the northwest cooled down first
options.rationale: Their age comes from when they formed over the hotspot.

options.label: Lava always flows downhill toward the northwest
options.rationale: Lava flow doesn't set island ages.

questions.explanation: The Pacific Plate moves over the hotspot, so volcanoes form over it and are carried off; the farther away, the older.

questions.prompt: What do the Hawaiian chain and Yellowstone's trail across Idaho have in common?

options.label: Both formed where two plates pull apart
Both are lines of volcanoes made by one giant eruption
options.rationale: Each line took millions of years to form.

options.label: Both record a plate sliding over a hotspot
Both get younger the farther you go from the hotspot

questions.explanation: In both, a plate moves over a hotspot and leaves a trail of volcanoes that gets older with distance.
